hook: On some toll roads, a ticket stamped at the entrance and the exit gives your average speed. If it says 75 miles per hour, the police know more than that: at some instant your speedometer read exactly 75. The Mean Value Theorem is the reason.

ideas: Mean Value Theorem: if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then $f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$ for at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$.
In words: somewhere inside, the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change.
"$f$ is differentiable" covers both hypotheses, because differentiable implies continuous. Say it.
The theorem says a $c$ exists. It does not say where, and there may be more than one.
A corner at an endpoint is fine: differentiability is needed only on the open interval.

misconception.wrong: The Mean Value Theorem works whenever the average rate of change can be computed.
misconception.right: It needs both hypotheses: continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. For $|x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ the average rate is $0$, but the slope is $\pm 1$ everywhere it exists. A justification must state the hypotheses before the conclusion.

summary: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, some $c$ inside has $f'(c)$ equal to the average rate of change: a tangent line parallel to the secant line. Check the hypotheses every time ("$f$ is differentiable, so it is continuous") and name the theorem.
